title: Gradient Routing Localizes and Removes Unintended Behaviors in RL
claim: Our gradient-routing method alone achieves high task performance with low unwanted behavior, while baseline mitigations fail or let the unwanted behavior re-emerge.
layout: 2 panels: left scatter with legend, right two stacked training-curve plots
description: The left panel is a scatter plot with reward hack rate on the x-axis (100% to 0%, so better is to the right) and clean-environment solve rate on the y-axis. Each method has a distinct marker and color, with error bars and faint per-run points. A legend lists no intervention, reward penalty, inoculation prompting, preventative steering, anchor environment only, GRAFT without routing, GRAFT (ours) and the base model. The green GRAFT dot sits in the top-right corner, the best region. The right side has two stacked line plots over 200 training steps. The top plot shows legitimate solve rate and the bottom shows reward hack rate. Each plot has green solid, blue dashed and red dotted curves with shaded bands, plus a gray dashed base-model line. Hack rate stays near zero for the green GRAFT curve.
caption: Gradient Routing Adapter Fine Tuning (GRAFT). Additional neurons are added to each MLP in a decoder-only Transformer; these are partitioned into a retain adapter and a forget adapter. When training in the target environment (left and center), both adapters are enabled ($\pi_{R+F}$) for the rollout phase and the actor update's forward pass. On trajectories not flagged by the monitor (left), both adapters receive gradient updates. On trajectories flagged by the monitor (center), only the forget adapter is updated and the gradient update to this adapter is amplified by a factor of 2. We concurrently train the model in a separate anchor environment where only the retain adapter is enabled ($\pi_R$) and updated (right).
abstract: We propose a mitigation to reward hacking in reinforcement learning. Our setup involves a misspecified reward function that gives rise to unintended behavior, and a monitor used to detect unintended behavior. As with frontier AI systems, the monitor makes systematic errors. Consequently, using the monitor for data filtering or to apply a reward penalty fails to prevent the model from learning unintended behavior ("reward hacking"). To address this problem, we introduce GRAFT: Gradient Routing Adapter Fine Tuning. Rather than penalizing or filtering flagged samples during training, GRAFT constrains gradient updates on those samples to a sacrificial set of new parameters. This has two benefits: First, because the monitor is not part of the reward function, the model does not learn to hide misbehavior. Second, ablating the sacrificial parameters reduces or entirely stops the unintended behavior while maintaining improved performance on target tasks. We demonstrate these benefits in RL environments where reward penalties cause models to learn to reward hack in undetected ways, training models ranging from 135M to 8B parameters. Additionally, we show a similar effect at a larger scale by distilling frontier LLM trajectories containing reward hacking into Qwen3-32B, without teaching that model to reward hack. Overall, our work suggests GRAFT may be a promising approach for leveraging imperfect monitors during post-training in settings where true performance is difficult to evaluate.
